Yeah but I suck at it. My main outlet is software so I DIY specifically when I want to try another skill I'm unfamiliar with. I never stick to the same skill because that's not the point for me. Leads to some pretty amateur electronics and carpentry. I mean amateur.

I've always been a DIY, Maker, Hacker fanatic, even if health problems have often gotten in my way. I think a lot of people frustrate themselves starting in DIY because, not being too familiar with all their options, they tend to pick things with a pretty high up-front proficiency/skill requirement or a need for more space and tools than they have. Men especially seem to think they are born with an inherent knowledge of all tools and construction. In reality, most Americans have a pretty low industrial literacy. As far as most of us are concerned, the supermarket gets restocked each night by Santa Claus and his Chinese elves. (though Chinese Santa is pretty kick-ass) Home improvement stores often exacerbate the problem as they're so focused on home improvement for the stick frame home and don't often carry the kind of products that would really make life easier for the DIY beginner. Though some big name stores produce books and run classes, there's a definite lack of learning aids in these stores--and a lot of people just won't read anyway. There are no good guides for the vast assortment of fasteners and hardware out there that can make things so much easier if only you knew about them and what their crazy names were. Things like rivkles (blind rivet nuts), fixing bolts, Garnier limbs (a big deal if you're into serious treehouses), Lamelo Invis magnetically driven screws and lock-pins, all that awesome marine rigging hardware like swages and toggles and turnbuckles. It is definitely getting better, though, now that so many people are sharing their knowledge by video on-line.

I've long been interested in the problems of the solitary homebuilder and the design of furnitecture (furniture that bridges the line between furniture and architecture through the use of multi-functional volumetric structures) and I like using techniques that will minimize that skill overhead, compensate for imprecision, minimize the need for messier stuff like paint and varnish, use more-or-less pre-finished or unfinished materials, and still produce good-looking results. For instance, simple modular techniques like the Matrix building system based on 'trilap' assembly. (which later became Box Beam and Gridbeam) Or the use of T-slot framing, electrical enclosure and retail display framing systems (though they can sometimes be expensive), pipe-fitting/clamp systems, or roadcase/flightcase hardware and materials. Roadcase making is an especially practical skill for makers and hackers that you can't find anything for in a typical hardware store. Painting is a particular problem for me as I'm sensitive to the chemicals fumes, but it's generally a pain in the ass and a hinderance to recycling things. Plenty of ways to go without it. With CNC and laser cutters slowly coming down in price and cutting services expanding in availability you can let computers eliminate a lot of skill overhead now too. Typical laser cut materials like basswood and MDF are completely paint-optional and look quite nice right out of the machines. Sure, if you're pursuing a specific handcraft, you're committing to a learning process, but it's getting much easier to make what you need to get the job done without a lot of skill. People just don't know their options.
